newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Black group wins Johnnic in landmark deal.
newsitem.headline: Black group wins Johnnic in landmark deal.

text.p: Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd said on Wednesday it was selling the bulk of its stake in Johnnies Industrial Corp Ltd (Johnnic) to black investors in a landmark deal for black economic empowerment.

South Africa's National Empowerment Consortium (NEC), representing 50 black economic interest groups, is to take up 41 percent of the industrial holding group in a deal worth over three billion rand ($670 million).

The NEC will purchase an initial shareholding of at least 20 percent in Johnnic at 50 rand per share -- against a current price of 56 rand -- and will have an 18-month option to take its stake to 35 percent.
A further six percent will be made available via a retail offering by the NEC to smaller NEC members and others within the black community.

"It is good to be here on a day when we witness an historic event where a grouping that represents (black interests) are entering into an agreement to take part ownership of a major organisation," said NEC chief negotiator Cyril Ramaphosa.
"This transaction in many ways deepens and enhances the whole process of black economic empowerment."

Anglo, which said late in 1994 that it intended to sell off its 47.4 percent stake in Johnnic held with associate diamond giant De Beers, said the deal with the NEC met its criteria for black economic empowerment.

"The fact that we came out with this conclusion bodes extremely well for partnership between ourselves and NEC and also bodes well for South Africa and its determination to be a winning nation," Anglo deputy chairman Nicky Oppenheimer said at a joint news conference with the NEC.

Johnnic's board of directors is to be reconstituted to comprise 20 members, of whom 10 will be nominated by the NEC, putting black hands firmly on the tiller of a group which itself controls key elements of the South African economy.

Johnnic's assets include a 13.9 percent stake in South African Breweries, 26.4 percent in Toyota South Africa, 27.5 percent in Premier Group and 43.0 percent of Omni Media, which controls Times Media.

The NEC said it would not be giving any contractual undertakings on editorial independence for Times Media titles, which include Business Day, Financial Mail and Sunday Times. But it said it would discuss the issue of assuring independence with editorial staff.
The deal is conditional on regulatory assurances that the NEC will not have to make a comparable offer to other Johnnic shareholders should it acquire a stake of 35 percent or more.

The NEC will also have until October 28 to conduct a due diligence investigation into the affairs of Johnnic, which on Wednesday reported a 41 percent jump in earnings to 489.5 million rand in the six months to June 30 from 346.4 million a year ago.
During that period to October 28 the NEC will also finalise the funding required for the purchase of the initial tranche of Johnnic shares.
Ramaphosa said he was confident the funds would be raised by the NEC, whose members include leading black businessman Nthato Motlana's New Africa Investments (NAIL) and several leading trade unions.
